emotions.name: Anger
emotions.definition: Anger can arise when an important goal is blocked, when you or someone you care about is attacked or threatened, or when power, status, or respect is lost.
fit_facts: An important goal is blocked or a desired activity is interrupted or prevented.
You or someone you care about is attacked, hurt, insulted, or threatened.
The integrity or status of your social group is offended or threatened.
opposite_actions: gently avoid instead of attacking
take a time out and breathe slowly
act kindly instead of being mean
unclench hands, jaw, chest, and stomach
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: An important goal is blocked or events do not turn out as expected.
You or someone you care about is attacked, threatened, or hurt.
You lose power, status, or respect.
interpretations: Believing you were treated unfairly or that important goals are being blocked.
Blaming, judging the situation as wrong or illegitimate, or rigidly thinking I am right.
Replaying the event that triggered the anger.
expressions_actions: Attacking or threatening, pounding or breaking things, stomping or slamming doors, walking out, criticizing, complaining, swearing, speaking loudly or sarcastically, frowning, crying, brooding, or withdrawing.
aftereffects: Attention narrows around the provoking event. You may ruminate about this or earlier situations, imagine future anger-provoking events, or experience numbness or dissociation.

emotions.name: Disgust
emotions.definition: Disgust can arise around possible contamination or around people and actions judged as deeply harmful or violating Wise Mind values.
fit_facts: Something you are in contact with could poison or contaminate you.
A person's behaviour could seriously damage or harm you or a group you belong to.
opposite_actions: move closer when it is safe
act kindly rather than with contempt
take in sensory information
relax the face, hands, chest, and stomach
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Encountering waste, dirt, blood, a dead body, an unwanted taste, or something experienced as contaminating.
Witnessing hypocrisy, betrayal, abuse, racism, cruelty, degradation, or unwanted sexual contact.
Confronting conduct that deeply violates Wise Mind values.
interpretations: Believing something is toxic or contaminating, judging a body as ugly, viewing a person as evil or immoral, feeling morally superior, or intensely disapproving of your own thoughts, feelings, or behaviour.
expressions_actions: Looking away, vomiting or spitting out, washing or changing clothes, cleaning, avoiding food, pushing or kicking away, fleeing, attacking, cursing, clenching, frowning, or speaking with contempt.
aftereffects: Attention stays fixed on what feels offensive or contaminating. The experience may be remembered vividly and can increase avoidance, rejection, or sensitivity to similar cues.

emotions.name: Envy
emotions.definition: Envy can arise when another person or group has something you want or need and do not have.
fit_facts: Another person or group gets or has something you want or need and do not have.
opposite_actions: do not destroy what another person has
count your blessings without discounting them
check facts about the other person's situation
relax the body
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Someone has something you want or receives recognition, advantage, success, or attention you wanted.
You compare yourself with someone who seems to have more.
interpretations: Thinking you deserve what the other person has, that their advantage is unfair, that you are inferior or unlucky, or that you will not get what you need unless it is taken from them.
expressions_actions: Competing, trying to take or spoil what another has, criticizing or gossiping, looking for the other person's faults, withdrawing, or repeatedly comparing.
aftereffects: Resentment and comparison can persist, pleasure in your own life may narrow, and you may keep scanning for evidence that others have more.

emotions.name: Fear
emotions.definition: Fear can arise in response to a threat to your life, health, or well-being, or to that of someone you care about.
fit_facts: There is a threat to your life or the life of someone you care about.
There is a threat to your health or well-being, or to that of someone you care about.
opposite_actions: approach what is safe instead of avoiding
look around and take in information
use a confident posture and voice
use paced breathing
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: A threat to your life, health, well-being, or that of someone you care about.
An unfamiliar situation, possible loss, public scrutiny, or cues associated with earlier danger.
interpretations: Believing you may be harmed, lose something important, fail, be rejected, be unable to cope, or that catastrophe is likely.
expressions_actions: Fleeing, freezing, hiding, avoiding, talking nervously, screaming, crying, asking for help or reassurance, scanning the surroundings, or preparing to defend yourself.
aftereffects: Threat cues remain vivid, the body may stay activated, and avoidance can make future fear more likely. Relief after escape can reinforce avoiding.

emotions.name: Happiness
emotions.definition: Happiness can arise when something wanted or unexpectedly good happens, a goal is achieved, connection is felt, or a pleasant experience is noticed.
fit_facts: A wanted or unexpectedly good event occurs, a goal is achieved, or a pleasant connection or sensation is present.
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Receiving something wanted, achieving a goal, being accepted or respected, enjoying a pleasant sensation or activity, connecting with people, or noticing that feared outcomes did not occur.
interpretations: Believing that something good has happened, needs have been met, a goal is within reach, the moment is safe, or possibilities are opening.
expressions_actions: Smiling, laughing, brightening the voice, moving energetically, sharing good news, expressing affection or gratitude, celebrating, and engaging more fully.
aftereffects: Positive expectations, openness, generosity, confidence, and willingness to connect or pursue goals may increase.

emotions.name: Jealousy
emotions.definition: Jealousy can arise when a valued relationship or object is in danger of being damaged or lost, especially when a rival seems involved.
fit_facts: A very important and desired relationship or object is in danger of being damaged or lost.
Someone is threatening to take a valued relationship or object away from you.
related_words: fear of losing someone or something
opposite_actions: let go of controlling others
share people and things in your life
stop spying or probing
take in all available information
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: An important relationship seems threatened by another person.
Someone you value gives time, attention, commitment, or affection to someone else.
interpretations: Believing a rival may take your place, that you are being rejected or betrayed, that the relationship is unstable, or that you are not valued enough.
expressions_actions: Interrogating, checking, spying, clinging, demanding reassurance, accusing, threatening a rival, trying to control contact, or withdrawing to test the relationship.
aftereffects: Suspicion and scanning may continue, trust can erode, and attempts to control the relationship can create the distance you fear.

emotions.name: Love
emotions.definition: Love can arise through affection, attraction, care, closeness, shared experience, or seeing a person, animal, object, place, or cause as deeply valuable.
fit_facts: Loving a person, animal, or object enhances quality of life for you or people you care about.
Loving increases your chances of attaining personal goals.
opposite_actions: avoid contact when love is not effective
distract from repeated thoughts
review the costs when those thoughts arise
adjust posture and distance
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Being with, thinking about, or receiving care from a person, animal, place, object, or cause you value; experiencing closeness, acceptance, shared meaning, or physical attraction.
interpretations: Believing someone is lovable, good, attractive, important, trustworthy, or in need of care; seeing the relationship as meaningful or beneficial.
expressions_actions: Approaching, touching, holding, spending time together, sharing, helping, protecting, expressing affection, and trying to please or maintain connection.
aftereffects: Attention returns to the loved person or object, separation may bring longing, and commitment, generosity, or vulnerability may increase.

emotions.name: Sadness
emotions.definition: Sadness can arise after an irreversible loss, separation, rejection, or when events are not what you wanted or expected.
fit_facts: You have lost something or someone permanently.
Things are not what you wanted or expected and hoped them to be.
opposite_actions: get active and approach
avoid avoiding
build mastery
increase pleasant events
attend to the present moment
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Losing someone or something permanently, not getting what was wanted or expected, feeling separated or rejected, or seeing another person's suffering.
interpretations: Believing a loss cannot be restored, that life will not improve, that you are alone, or that important goals are out of reach.
expressions_actions: Crying, speaking softly or little, frowning, slumping, moving slowly, withdrawing, giving up, seeking comfort, or talking about the loss.
aftereffects: Attention stays with the loss, positive events may be hard to notice, energy and motivation can remain low, and memories of other losses may surface.

emotions.name: Shame
emotions.definition: Shame can arise when you expect rejection if a characteristic of yourself or your behaviour becomes public; it often includes a global judgment about the self.
fit_facts: You will be rejected by a person or group you care about if characteristics of yourself or your behaviour are made public.
body_changes: wanting to hide the face or body
opposite_actions: when safe, share with people who will accept you
do not over-apologize for a perceived transgression
take in all the information
lift your head and keep a steady voice
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Being exposed or judged for something viewed as wrong, failing to meet personal or group standards, having private information revealed, or being rejected because of a characteristic or action.
interpretations: Judging yourself as bad, inferior, unlovable, defective, or outside the group; believing others will reject you if they know the truth.
expressions_actions: Hiding, avoiding eye contact, lowering the head, apologizing repeatedly, appeasing, withdrawing, attacking yourself, or trying to distract attention from the perceived flaw.
aftereffects: Self-focus and replaying the event may continue. Isolation can increase, and secrecy may prevent corrective experiences or effective repair.

emotions.name: Guilt
emotions.definition: Guilt can arise when your own behaviour violates your values or moral code; unlike shame's global self-judgment, guilt focuses on an action that may call for repair.
fit_facts: Your own behaviour violates your own values or moral code.
opposite_actions: when guilt does not fit, stop unnecessary apologies or repair attempts
take in all the information
use an upright posture and steady voice
emotions.source_reference: Emotion Regulation Handout 6; Emotion Regulation Handout 11 where available
prompting_events: Doing or failing to do something that violates your values, causes harm, breaks a commitment, or falls short of a responsibility.
interpretations: Believing your behaviour was wrong, that you are responsible for harm, or that you should have acted differently. Guilt focuses on an action; global judgments about being a bad person move toward shame.
expressions_actions: Apologizing, confessing, explaining, making amends, trying to repair, asking forgiveness, withdrawing, or repeatedly reviewing what happened.
aftereffects: Attention remains on the action and its consequences. Effective guilt can motivate repair; ineffective guilt can become rumination, avoidance, or self-punishment.
